---
title: "Coefficient inference"
description: "Conditional posterior draws, selected-support standard errors and bootstrap selection stability."
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE,comment='#>',message=FALSE,warning=FALSE)
```

L0glm provides conditional posterior summaries, selected-model standard errors
and bootstrap selection stability. These optional calculations are requested in
`summary()` and leave the fitted point estimates unchanged.

```{r fit}
library(L0glm)
set.seed(51)
X <- matrix(rnorm(200*10),200,10)
y <- 1+2*X[,1]-2*X[,2]+rnorm(200)
fit <- l0glmFit(X,y,intercept=TRUE,lambda='gic')
```

## Conditional posterior summaries and sampling

```{r posterior}
posterior <- summary(fit,inference='posterior',
  control.inference=list(nsim=2000L,seed=1))$inference
posterior$coefficients
posterior$prior.source
draws <- simulate(posterior,nsim=1000L,seed=2)
dim(draws)
```

An accepted full unpenalized support refit uses a flat prior. A fit that retains
adaptive-ridge shrinkage uses a frozen Gaussian prior, obtained by one inverse-square
update at its fitted coefficients. Mandatory coefficients have a flat prior;
`prior.mean` supplies the other prior centres. With selected coefficient support
\(J\), prior precision \(P\) and fitted noise parameters \(\widehat\psi\), the target is

\[
p(\beta_J\mid y,J,P,\widehat\psi)\propto
\exp\{\ell(\beta_J,\widehat\psi)-\tfrac12(\beta_J-c)^TP(\beta_J-c)\}
1_{\mathcal C}(\beta_J).
\]

The calculation finds a separate conditional mode with this prior and noise
held fixed. It uses a local Gaussian likelihood approximation, with the full
coefficient covariance. Nonnegative coefficients are sampled from a truncated
joint Gaussian. Multinomial draws preserve the zero-sum CLR constraints.
For Gaussian identity models with known dispersion, the frozen-prior Gaussian
calculation is exact, including its truncation.

The table reports the original estimates, conditional modes, posterior means,
standard deviations and equal-tail credible limits. Sparse draws retain the
original coefficient dimensions, with excluded entries zero. `simulate(fit,...)`
constructs the posterior directly; `simulate(posterior,...)` reuses its stored
information without retaining a copy of the training data.

Cholesky sampling and independent rejection are used when practical. Native
Gibbs sampling handles more restrictive nonnegative regions. For a Gibbs run,
increase `burnin` or `thin` and compare seeds when posterior correlations are
strong. `max.parameters` and `max.cells` bound the information and draw storage.

## Selected-support standard errors

```{r conditional}
details <- summary(fit,inference='conditional')
details$inference$coefficients
```

The selected coefficients are refitted without a sparsity penalty, with their
observation weights, offsets and coefficient constraints retained. The table
includes both the selected point estimates and the refitted estimates, standard
errors, intervals and Wald tests. The original fitted model is preserved.

Gaussian and other ordinary GLMs use model-based information; estimated scales
use selected-model Pearson dispersion. Negative binomial models retain fixed
shape or reestimate it as specified. Multinomial covariance is computed on its
selected zero-sum subspace and returned in CLR coordinates. Cox inference uses
weighted Breslow partial-likelihood information. Nonnegative boundaries and
singular information receive unavailable ordinary Wald standard errors.

The nominal fixed-model interpretation treats the chosen support as given.
When support recovery is reliable, it approaches the ordinary inference problem
with the correct model. Selection itself can add substantial uncertainty near
detection thresholds.

## Bootstrap selection stability

```{r bootstrap, eval=FALSE}
uncertainty <- summary(fit,inference='bootstrap',
  control.inference=list(nboot=199L,seed=1))
uncertainty$inference$coefficients
uncertainty$inference$diagnostics
```

Each replicate resamples observation rows and their weights and offsets, then
reruns the saved fit specification, including SIS/ISIS, interaction generation
and local support refinement. Starting exclusions remain fixed as specified.
Intervals include zero estimates when a coefficient is absent. Sparse draws and
selection frequencies retain every original predictor, with a shared union of
generated interaction terms. Failed fits, solver warnings, convergence and
timings are recorded.

A supplied seed preserves the caller's random-number state. The default memory
guard prevents large dense row-resampling blocks; `max.cells` can be set explicitly
when the required memory is available. Predictors are kept eligible throughout
the resampling procedure according to their original starting restrictions.

A model extracted from `l0glmTune()` retains its chosen penalty for this bootstrap.
A `refit` callback can repeat tuning within each replicate:

```{r retune, eval=FALSE}
retune <- function(args) {
  args$lambda <- NULL
  args$family <- gaussian()
  do.call(l0glmTune,c(args,list(tune='cv',nfolds=5L,nlambda=10L,
    plot=FALSE,printbest=FALSE)))$fit_best
}
uncertainty <- summary(fit,inference='bootstrap',
  control.inference=list(nboot=199L,seed=1,refit=retune))
```

Bootstrap intervals describe resampling variability. Near selection thresholds,
ordinary bootstrap and fixed-model intervals can have imperfect nominal coverage;
selection frequencies are useful stability diagnostics, rather than a proof that
the selected support is correct. See the
[reference page](../reference/coefficient_inference.html) for covariance formulas,
controls and the discussion by [Leeb and Poetscher (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2007.05.017).

## Frequentist coverage in deconvolution

A 95% conditional credible interval need not cover a fixed true coefficient in
95% of repeated datasets after variable selection. Shifted PSF columns are highly
correlated: omitted neighbouring peaks can bias retained coefficients, and an
estimated adaptive prior introduces additional shrinkage. Dispersion and support
uncertainty are held fixed in the posterior calculation.

The following experiments use nonnegative GIC-preset deconvolution. Single-channel
designs have 1,000 scans, 1,000 predictors and 100 peaks, with 200 repeated noise
draws. Three-channel designs have 500 scans, 500 predictors and 50 shared peaks,
with 100 repeats. Gaussian noise has SD 5; Poisson means use the simulated signal.
Each interval uses 2,000 coefficient draws. The reference fits restrict the design
to the true predictors.

| Noise and model | Coverage among recovered true coefficients | Coverage across all true coefficients | True-predictor reference |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| Poisson, single channel | 74.0% | 62.3% | 94.9% |
| Gaussian, known variance, single channel | 79.5% | 71.2% | 94.7% |
| Gaussian, estimated variance, single channel | 81.8% | 74.4% | 94.7% |
| Poisson, three channels | 86.2% | 74.8% | 94.2% |
| Gaussian, known variance, three channels | 87.7% | 84.4% | 95.2% |
| Gaussian, estimated variance, three channels | 91.4% | 90.0% | 95.3% |

The second column conditions on recovery at the exact predictor location. The
third also counts missed peaks as uncovered. Monte Carlo standard errors for
the recovered-coefficient coverage are about 0.2–0.4 percentage points across
replicates. All runs completed successfully. These results support using the
intervals to describe uncertainty within the selected model; they do not provide
selection-adjusted confidence guarantees. The bootstrap additionally describes
selection stability, with its own coverage considerations near thresholds.

[Reproduce the coverage experiments](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/benchmarks/benchmark_posterior_coverage.R).

Reducing peak heights twentyfold gives recovered-coefficient coverage of 67.1%
for Poisson and 71.1% for Gaussian noise with estimated variance in the
single-channel experiment. The true-predictor references give 92.6% and 94.6%,
respectively. The reproducible benchmark includes these lower-signal cases.
